Course · Whole course on one page

From zero to a chip: FPGA programming with t27

No hardware background needed. Every lesson opens a real tool built from real runs on our bench: read a little, then try it yourself.

27 lessons, one working widget and one t27 spec each: what an FPGA is, how numbers become bits, your own t27 spec, how t27c compiles it, and how it becomes a bitstream on a real board.

Every course is free, for everyone: no sign-up, no email, nothing to pay.

01

Module 1 · The chip

What an FPGA is, which chip we use, and how its pins meet the board.

01

Lesson 1 of 27

An FPGA is a grid you configure

You will learnWhat an FPGA is made of, and why a design uses only part of the chip.

A CPU runs instructions one after another. An FPGA has no program at all: it is a grid of small blocks -- lookup tables (LUTs), flip-flops, carry chains, block RAM and DSP multipliers -- joined by wires you can switch. Configuring the grid builds a circuit. Our bench chip is an AMD Artix-7 XC7A200T. The skyline draws one routed design on that die: every tile it configures stands up as a column, and most of the chip stays dark.

Try it

Rotate the die and tap the tallest column: which kind of tile sets the most features? In the spec frame of our bench board, find LUT_TOTAL, then the invariant on DSP48E1_TOTAL: what does its name say our cores use?

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Lesson 2 of 27

Which chip is this?

You will learnHow a chip names itself in 32 bits, and how to read those bits.

Before you load anything, you ask the board which chip it has. Over JTAG every chip answers with a 32-bit IDCODE: a version, a part number, the manufacturer and a fixed 1 in bit 0. A bitstream built for the wrong part is refused by the chip, so this is the check that saves you an afternoon. The decoder splits the bits into those four fields and looks the part up in openFPGALoader's own table.

Try it

Click the bench preset, then flip one bit of the part number and see which device it would be. In the spec frame, the idcode-cfg action names the IDCODE a healthy XC7A100T returns: decode it and compare its part number with the bench chip's.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Lesson 3 of 27

Pins, balls and the package

You will learnHow the signals of your design reach the outside world.

A chip sits in a package: the XC7A200T on our board has 676 solder balls under it. Some carry power or configuration and only some are user IO, grouped into banks with their own voltage. A constraints file (XDC) says which ball each signal of your design uses. Put a signal on a ball that is not user IO and the build fails, or worse, the board does not do what you think.

Try it

Search for a ball name like E3, then colour by pin type and find a ball that is not user IO. The spec frame pins a small design to another package, the XC7A100T in CSG324: find the test that puts its clock on ball E3, and the one that counts its pins.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Module 2 · Numbers in hardware

Bits, trits and number formats, and what arithmetic costs in logic.

04

Lesson 4 of 27

Bits, trits and GF16

You will learnHow a number is stored in bits, and how balanced ternary stores it in trits.

Hardware stores numbers as fixed groups of bits, and t27 makes you write the width: u8 is 8 unsigned bits, i16 is 16 signed bits. t27 also speaks balanced ternary, where a trit is -1, 0 or +1. For fractions it has GF16, a 16-bit float with 1 sign bit, 6 exponent bits and 9 mantissa bits. Type a number into the calculator and watch how it is rounded, field by field, and how big the error is.

Try it

Type 1.618 and read the exponent and mantissa bits; then type 0.1 and look at the error.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Lesson 5 of 27

What arithmetic costs

You will learnWhy a multiplier is expensive and an adder is cheap, measured on a real chip.

In logic, every operation has a price paid in chip resources. An adder is a carry chain, cheap and fast. A multiplier built from LUTs is large; the chip has DSP blocks made for multiplying, and a synthesizer uses them when it may. These curves are real yosys counts from 4 to 64 bits. Switch DSPs off and on, and see why hardware people care so much about the width of every number.

Try it

Pick Multiply, switch DSP48E1 to -nodsp, and compare the LUTs at 32 bits with and without DSPs.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Lesson 6 of 27

How much fits on the chip

You will learnHow to read a resource count and find which resource runs out first.

A synthesis report says how many LUTs, flip-flops, DSPs and block RAMs your design takes. The question that matters is which of them runs out first. A design can use few LUTs and still not fit because it needs more DSPs than the chip has. Type a LUT count, or pick one of our real designs, and see how many copies fit on an XC7A200T.

Try it

Pick a real design, then raise the DSP count until something other than LUTs runs out first. In the spec frame, fits_board checks four resources in turn: which one comes last, and how many DSP48 blocks does xc7a100t_resources list?

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Module 3 · Your t27 program

Write a spec, test it, and see why compiling is not the same as being right.

07

Lesson 7 of 27

Hello, t27

You will learnWhat a t27 spec looks like, and what the compiler does with it in your browser.

A t27 program is a spec: a module with typed constants, functions and tests. Prose lines start with a semicolon at the start of a line. The player below runs the real t27 compiler, built to WebAssembly, inside your browser: it reads hello_world.t27, runs its tests and writes code for seven backends. Nothing is installed and nothing is sent anywhere. Open the tutorial spec under the widget and read it next to the output.

Try it

Run the tests in the player, then switch the backend and find the same function in two languages.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Lesson 8 of 27

Tests are part of the spec

You will learnWhy every t27 spec carries its own tests, and what a waveform shows.

In t27 a spec is not finished without its claims: test blocks, invariants and benches live in the same file as the code they check, and the compiler refuses a spec with none. A test can also be run as gates in a simulator. The waves below are a real simulation of Verilog generated from a ternary multiply-accumulate spec, driven by that spec's own test vectors.

Try it

Zoom into one clock cycle and read the values on the buses at a pass mark.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Lesson 9 of 27

Compiles is not the same as correct

You will learnWhy green checks are not proof, and how to catch code that compiles and is wrong.

A compiler that accepts your code only tells you the code is well formed. It does not tell you the code means what you meant. This recording shows a tool that found specs which compile, pass every gate and are still read wrongly. The lesson for hardware is sharper still: a bug in silicon cannot be patched. Plant a bug yourself in the mutation recording and watch the tests catch it.

Try it

Open the mutation recording under Also try and count how many planted bugs the tests caught.

04

Module 4 · Inside t27c

How the compiler reads a spec and what it writes, including the native t27b.

10

Lesson 10 of 27

The stages of t27c

You will learnThe path a spec takes inside t27c: tokens, syntax tree, types, HIR, code.

t27c reads a spec in stages. The lexer cuts the text into tokens. The parser builds a syntax tree. The type checker checks every width and every call. The tree is lowered to HIR, a simpler form, and each backend writes code from it. This widget runs those stages on a spec in your browser and shows what each one produced, so an error has a stage you can point at.

Try it

Pick an example and step through the stages; find the stage where a type error would stop.

Open the interactive lesson →
11

Lesson 11 of 27

t27c on a real machine

You will learnThe same compiler on a real machine, printing what it really prints.

The player in lesson 7 runs the compiler in your browser. This recording is the native t27c, written in Rust, run on a real machine on the same hello_world.t27: it reports the spec's status, the tests and invariants it emits, and the Verilog module with its parameters. Every byte in the recording was printed by the command; only the typing is staged.

Try it

Find the line where t27c prints the Verilog module's parameters.

Open the interactive lesson →
12

Lesson 12 of 27

Seven backends, and t27b

You will learnOne spec, many target languages, and a native compiler with no LLVM.

One t27 spec can become Zig, C, Rust, JavaScript, TypeScript or Verilog; Verilog comes two ways, straight from the spec and through the HIR, which makes seven backends. The player shows the Rust t27c writes for hello_world. t27b is a second compiler: native AArch64 machine code, no LLVM, a JIT for tests and Mach-O object files. It is not finished, and we say how far it is: in run 26c447ad8 it passed 307 of the 449 specs that the reference compiler passes with tests, 68.4%.

Try it

Switch the player to JavaScript under Also try, generate the module, and run it.

05

Module 5 · From spec to hardware

The Verilog t27c writes, the cells it becomes, and what one LUT does.

13

Lesson 13 of 27

From a spec to Verilog

You will learnHow a t27 function becomes logic, and how a clocked function becomes registers.

Verilog is the text a synthesizer reads to build a circuit. t27c writes it from the spec. A function named on_clock becomes an always block on the clock edge, and every module var becomes a register with a reset. Open clocked_counter.t27 in the player: an 8-bit counter in a few lines, and the Verilog it turns into. Its header records what yosys built from it.

Try it

Open clocked_counter.t27 in the player and find the always block in its Verilog tab.

Open the interactive lesson →
14

Lesson 14 of 27

Count the cells

You will learnHow to count what a synthesizer built: LUTs, flip-flops, DSPs, block RAM.

After synthesis, yosys can print what it built as JSON: how many LUTs, flip-flops, DSPs and block RAMs. Those counts are an honest measure of a design before place and route. Paste a stat -json from yosys into the stat card, or open the real sample, and get a card and a README badge that say plainly that they are a synthesis count.

Try it

Open the real sample, then read the LUT and FF counts on the card.

Open the interactive lesson →
15

Lesson 15 of 27

One LUT, up close

You will learnWhat a 6-input lookup table is, and how 64 bits describe any gate.

A LUT6 is a tiny memory with 6 address inputs and 64 one-bit entries. Any logic function of 6 inputs is just its truth table written into those 64 bits, the INIT value. Paste an INIT and the widget reads it back as a truth table and an expression. Then play the guessing game on LUTs taken from a real routed design: XOR, AND, a multiplexer, or something with no short name.

Try it

Try the XOR6 and majority examples, then play five rounds of Guess the gate. In the spec frame, full_adder is built from xor2 and maj3: which one makes the carry, and how many neurons does the spec say it takes?

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Module 6 · Reading synthesis

What yosys reports about your design, and which warnings matter.

16

Lesson 16 of 27

Synthesis warnings that matter

You will learnHow to read a yosys log, and the warnings that become bugs on silicon.

yosys tells you a lot, and most of it is fine. A few lines are not: a latch you did not mean, a wire nothing drives, two drivers on one net, a memory that became flip-flops. Each of those works in simulation and fails on the chip. Open one of the real logs from t27 specs, then paste a log of your own.

Try it

Open each real log and find the one that yosys refused, and why. In the spec frame, a cross-module pass counts what it cleaned up: find the three counters of CrossOptPass and the test where they add up to 17.

Open the interactive lesson →
17

Lesson 17 of 27

State machines

You will learnHow a synthesizer finds a state machine in your design, or refuses to.

Many designs are state machines: a register that holds the current state and logic that picks the next one. yosys looks for them and, when it finds one, can re-encode it. When it refuses, it says why. The widget draws the graph yosys extracted from real designs, a UART receiver and a SPI flash master, and shows a case it refused.

Try it

Open the uart_rx sample and count its states and transitions. The JTAG port runs a state machine too: in the spec frame, find the test that says how many states the TAP controller has.

Open the interactive lesson →
18

Lesson 18 of 27

Where the LUTs go

You will learnWhich part of a design spends the LUTs, and why hierarchy matters.

A design is built from modules that contain modules. When yosys keeps the hierarchy, it counts each submodule once, and the instance counts tell you how many copies there are. The treemap multiplies them out and shows which submodule eats the LUTs. One adder used many times can cost more than everything else together.

Try it

Switch between the hierarchical and flattened totals and find the largest tile. In the spec frame, find fpga_util and the test that turns 31700 used LUTs into a share of one chip: what percent does it get?

Open the interactive lesson →
07

Module 7 · Place, route, timing

Where the cells land on the die, and whether the clock is met.

19

Lesson 19 of 27

Placement: where the cells land

You will learnWhat place and route does, and where it put a real design.

Synthesis says which cells you need. Place and route decides where each one sits on the die and which wires connect them. nextpnr-xilinx does both in the open flow. The map draws every placed cell of a real run on the XC7A200T: a small design is a small cluster in a huge chip.

Try it

Fit the design, then tap cells of different types and read their BEL names. In the spec frame, find RegionKind: which two of its five kinds are columns, and which test checks that a BRAM column is 1 wide?

Open the interactive lesson →
20

Lesson 20 of 27

Logic depth

You will learnWhy the longest chain of logic sets how fast a design can run.

A signal needs time to pass through each LUT and each wire. The longest chain of logic between two registers sets how fast the clock can tick. yosys can show that chain as a count of cells, before any routing. The staircase draws it for a real GF16 adder, step by step.

Try it

Open the real sample and count how many steps of the path are LUTs. In the spec frame, est_comb_delay charges each LUT 100 ps plus 300 ps of routing: find the test that gets 600 for three LUTs.

Open the interactive lesson →
21

Lesson 21 of 27

Timing and slack

You will learnWhat slack is, and how to read a timing report path by path.

Slack is how much time is left on a path when the clock period ends. Positive slack: the path is fast enough. Negative: the design fails at that clock. Each bar here is a real path from a routed design at 50 MHz, split into logic and routing, worst first. Find where the time goes on the worst path.

Try it

Click the worst path and compare its logic time with its routing time. In the spec frame, every clock_tree carries 100 ps of skew: find the test where a 50 ps budget fails, and the one where 200 ps passes.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Module 8 · The bitstream

How a routed design becomes the bits the chip loads, with no Vivado.

22

Lesson 22 of 27

From FASM to frames

You will learnWhat FASM is, and how features become configuration frames.

After routing, the design is a list of features to switch on, in a text format called FASM: this LUT has this INIT, this wire connects to that one. Tools from prjxray turn features into configuration frames, blocks of bits the chip loads. This recording does that step with t27's own tool and compares every frame with the reference tool: they are byte-identical.

Try it

Find where the recording says how many frames matched, out of how many. In the spec frame, HELP_LINE says what tri x7-fasm compares against fasm2frames: of its 20 entries, how many are real and how many must be refused?

Open the interactive lesson →
23

Lesson 23 of 27

A build, itemised

You will learnEvery stage from a spec to a bitstream, with its time, tool and hash.

A whole build from a t27 spec to an Artix-7 bitstream, written out like a shop receipt: each stage, the tool and its version, the time it took, and the sha256 of what it wrote. No Vivado anywhere. When a number on a receipt can be checked, anyone can rebuild it and compare the hash.

Try it

Read the receipt: which stage took the longest, and which tool ran it? In the spec frame, RECEIPT_KINDS names two kinds of receipt: which one is the build alone, and which entry in ERRORS catches it posing as the other?

Open the interactive lesson →
24

Lesson 24 of 27

Read a bitstream

You will learnWhat is inside a .bit file, and which chip it was built for.

A .bit file is a header followed by packets: commands to the chip's configuration logic and the frames themselves. One of those commands writes the IDCODE of the chip the file was built for. Drop a .bit into the autopsy and see which chip it asks for. Five bitstreams committed to t27 turn out to target a different part than our bench.

Try it

Open the blink_j26 sample and compare the part in its header with the IDCODE it writes. In the spec frame, read HELP_LINE: against which reference tool is tri x7-writer byte-identical, and what kind of input does it refuse?

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Module 9 · On the board

Ask the chip who it is, load the bits, and check them.

25

Lesson 25 of 27

JTAG asks the chip

You will learnHow a cable finds the chip on a board and reads its IDCODE.

JTAG is the cable protocol for talking to the chip on a board. Before programming, the tool shifts out the IDCODE of every device on the chain. This recording decodes the codes our bench answers with, and shows what an even code means: no IDCODE at all. Compare it with the decoder from lesson 2.

Try it

Find which IDCODE belongs to an XC7A200T and which to an XC7A100T. In the spec frame, HELP_LINE says how tri fpga-jtag reads a chain with no answer: what does it blame for all ones, and what for all zeros?

Open the interactive lesson →
26

Lesson 26 of 27

The same bits, on the board

You will learnHow to show that a bitstream is byte-identical and that it runs.

The claim most FPGA people doubt: a bitstream built by an open flow from t27 specs, byte-identical to the reference toolchain, and working on a real board. This recording compares the files, loads the bits into the chip's SRAM and counts the receipts the board sends back. Drop two .bit files into bit-diff to check the byte-identical part yourself.

Try it

Wait for the receipts count at the end, then try bit-diff under Also try. In the spec frame, ACTIONS lists the steps of tri x7-board: which one loads the chip's SRAM, and which flag does HELP_LINE say it needs?

Open the interactive lesson →
27

Lesson 27 of 27

Capstone: out-guess yosys

You will learnPut it together: guess what a real t27 module costs in LUTs.

Everything from this course in one game. Each day Gatle shows one real t27 module and the Verilog your browser compiles from it; you have six guesses at how many LUTs yosys spent on it. Use what you know: widths, multipliers, hierarchy, state. Then look at the other ways people and agents compete on t27.

Try it

Play today's puzzle. Then read the module's Verilog and say why it cost what it did. Run the tests in the spec frame: how many of the 12 instructions in hello_kernel are GF16 operations, and which test says all 12 take 48 bytes?

TRI CLAW

The agent behind t27, in Telegram and on GitHub

TRI CLAW is the project's agent: it writes and checks .t27 specs with you. Three ways to use it.

  • Free, with your own key

    Add your own API key (NVIDIA or z.ai today) and the agent runs on it. Add more keys any time.

    Add a key in Telegram ↗

  • We do it for you

    No keys to keep: join the club in our Telegram bot and the agent runs on ours. The bot shows the price before you pay.

    Join the club in Telegram ↗

  • On GitHub

    TRI CLAW is also a GitHub App, built to check the .t27 specs a pull request changes. It is not open to other repositories yet.

    Read about TRI CLAW ↗
